unit.title: Support continuous improvement systems and processes

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

Managers alone deciding all changes

Regular small changes, tested and kept if they work

essays.stem: Explain the PDCA cycle step by step, using the example of cutting the fit-up time for a batch of repeat gate frames.
essays.modelAnswer: Continuous improvement means making small, tested changes all the time. PDCA gives the steps. Plan: the team measures the present fit-up time for a gate frame, say 40 minutes, and watches how it is done. It finds the causes of delay, for example measuring every piece by hand and re-squaring the frame several times. It sets a target, such as 25 minutes, and plans a change: a simple jig with stops and clamps. Do: the jig is made and tried on a small number of frames, with the welders trained to use it, and the times and dimensions are recorded. Check: the team compares the new times and the accuracy with the baseline. If the frames now take 25 minutes and are square, the change works; if not, the team finds out why. Act: if it works, the jig and method are written into the procedure, everyone is trained and the jig is checked regularly. Then the cycle starts again with the next problem.
markingPoints: Explains continuous improvement as small, tested changes
Plan: measure baseline, find causes, set target, plan change
Do: trial on a small scale and record results
Check: compare with the baseline and find why if not improved
Act: standardise, train and maintain, then repeat the cycle

essays.stem: Last quarter the inspector recorded 50 weld defects: porosity 20, undercut 12, lack of fusion 8, slag inclusions 6 and wrong size 4. Put them in Pareto order, work out the share of the top two, and explain what the team should do next.
essays.modelAnswer: In Pareto order, from most to least, the defects are porosity 20, undercut 12, lack of fusion 8, slag inclusions 6 and wrong size 4, which adds up to 50. The top two together are 20 + 12 = 32 defects, and 32 ÷ 50 × 100 = 64% of all defects. So most of the problem comes from two causes, and the team should work on these first. For porosity, the team could draw a fishbone diagram and check the likely causes: damp electrodes, dirty or oily plate, draughts blowing away the shielding gas, a gas leak or wrong flow rate, and a long arc. For undercut, it could check current, travel speed and electrode angle. The team would agree one or two changes, such as an electrode oven and a plate-cleaning step, trial them, and record defects again for a month to compare with the baseline. If they work, they become the standard method.
markingPoints: Correct Pareto order: porosity, undercut, lack of fusion, slag, wrong size
Top two = 32 of 50 = 64%
Explains that work should start on the top causes
Uses a tool such as a fishbone to find the root causes, with sensible causes
Trial, measure against the baseline, then standardise

essays.stem: Porosity keeps appearing in MIG welds on a production line. Describe a fishbone diagram for this problem, with its main branches and likely causes, and explain how the team would find which cause is the real one.
essays.modelAnswer: The problem, 'porosity in MIG welds', goes at the head of the fish. The main bones could be people, method, machine, materials and environment. People: welders not trained on gas flow or holding the gun too far away. Method: no plate cleaning step, wrong travel angle, too long a stick-out. Machine: gas leak in the hose or fittings, blocked or spattered nozzle, faulty regulator or flowmeter. Materials: rusty, oily or painted plate, damp or dirty wire, wrong or empty gas cylinder. Environment: fans or open doors blowing the gas shield away. The team would then check the likely causes with facts, not guesses. It could leak test the gas line, check the flow at the nozzle, look at the plate condition, and record where and when porosity happens. If porosity is worst near the open door on windy days, draught is likely. The team would test one change at a time, such as a screen, and see if porosity falls.
markingPoints: Problem at the head; sensible main branches
Likely causes under people and method
Likely causes under machine and materials
Environment causes such as draughts
Checks causes with data and tests one change at a time

essays.stem: A visitor walking through your shop sees welders walking back and forth to the store, frames waiting for the crane, and stacks of finished parts that no client has ordered. Name the kinds of waste these show, add one more of your own, and suggest an improvement for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Welders walking back and forth to the store is motion waste: people moving more than the work needs. An improvement is to kit the parts and consumables for each job before work starts, or keep common consumables at each bay. Frames waiting for the crane is waiting waste: work and people standing idle. The team could plan crane use with a daily schedule, or provide a small jib crane or trolley at the busiest bay. Stacks of parts no client has ordered is overproduction, which ties up steel and space and can lead to damage or rust. The shop should make parts to orders and the programme, in the batch sizes needed. My own example is defects: welds that must be ground out and redone, which waste time, rods and gas. The improvement is to find the root cause, for example by drying electrodes and cleaning plate, and to check the first part of each batch.
markingPoints: Motion, with a sensible improvement
Waiting, with a sensible improvement
Overproduction, with a sensible improvement
One more waste named correctly (defects, transport, inventory, over-processing or unused skills)
Improvement for the added waste

essays.stem: Explain how a jig or fixture can improve quality and productivity on repeat fabrication work, and how you would trial one and prove that it works.
essays.modelAnswer: A jig holds the parts in the right place while they are tacked and welded. Because every part goes against the same stops, the frames come out the same size and square, so there is less measuring, less rework and fewer rejects. It can also be designed so a part only fits the right way round, which prevents mistakes. Fit-up is faster, and less skilled workers can fit up accurately under supervision. A jig can also hold the work in a better position, which makes welding easier and safer. To trial one, I would first measure the baseline: the time per frame and the dimensions of, say, ten frames made the old way. Then I would make a simple jig, check it against the drawing, and use it on another ten frames, recording the same measures. If the time falls and the frames are more accurate, the jig works. I would also ask the welders how it could be better, then add it to the procedure and check its accuracy at set intervals.
markingPoints: Explains how a jig gives repeatable, accurate parts
Can prevent mistakes (parts fit only one way)
Faster fit-up and less rework; may improve welding position
Trial: baseline measures, then the same measures with the jig
Asks the welders, standardises and checks the jig regularly

essays.stem: Your shop's suggestion box has had no ideas in six months. Explain why this might be, and what you would do to get the welders and fitters involved in improvement.
essays.modelAnswer: There may be several reasons. Workers may think nobody reads the ideas, because past ideas got no answer. They may fear being laughed at or blamed, or think improvement is the managers' job. Some may find writing difficult, and others may be too busy with no time set aside. To change this, I would empty the box and answer every past idea, saying what will happen. I would make it easy to give ideas: a short talk at the weekly toolbox meeting, a board where ideas can be written or spoken to the team leader, not only written in a box. Each idea would get a reply within a week. Good ideas would be trialled with the person who suggested them, and the results shown on the board, with thanks and credit given in front of the team. Ideas that cannot be used would be explained, not ignored. I would also set a small, clear problem each month, such as reducing grinding time, and ask for ideas on it.
markingPoints: Gives likely reasons (no feedback, fear, not their job, literacy, no time)
Answers past ideas and gives quick replies
Makes it easy to give ideas in more than one way
Trials ideas with the person and shows results with credit
Explains rejected ideas and sets focused problems for ideas

essays.stem: After a successful trial, the shop will change from MMAW to flux-cored welding for its heavy frames. Explain how you would introduce the new method so that it is used correctly and kept up.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the change, I would make sure a welding procedure specification for the flux-cored process is written and qualified for the joints we make, and that each welder who will use it is tested and approved. The machines, wire feeders, gas and wire must be ready, and the store must stock the right wire. I would explain to the team why we are changing, for example faster welding and fewer stops, and show the results of the trial. Each welder would be trained and practise on test pieces before welding real frames, with fume extraction in place because flux-cored welding makes more fume. I would update the work instructions and remove the old ones for those frames. In the first weeks I would watch the work closely, check welds by inspection, and record repairs and welding times to compare with the trial. I would listen to concerns, fix problems quickly, and review the results with the team after a month.
markingPoints: Qualified WPS and approved welders before use
Equipment, consumables and stock ready
Explains the reason and shares trial results
Training and practice, with fume control; procedures updated and old ones removed
Close monitoring, measurement, listening to concerns and review

essays.stem: Explain how you would monitor an improvement after it has been put in place, using a run chart or control chart, and what you would do if the results began to slip.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would choose a clear measure that shows whether the improvement is working, such as weld repairs per 100 welds or minutes of fit-up per frame, and keep the baseline from before the change. I would record the measure at a set time each week and plot it on a run chart, or a control chart with a centre line and limits, on the board in the shop where everyone can see it. The chart shows trends better than single numbers: a steady fall shows the improvement is working, and a point outside the limits or a run of points going the wrong way shows something has changed. If results begin to slip, I would not just blame people. I would find out what changed: a new welder, a new batch of wire, a worn jig, or the new method not being followed. I would fix the cause, retrain if needed, and keep watching the chart. I would also set a review date to decide if more improvement is needed.
markingPoints: Chooses a clear measure and keeps the baseline
Records regularly and plots a run or control chart where all can see
Explains how to read trends and points outside limits
Investigates causes when results slip, without blame
Fixes the cause, retrains, keeps monitoring and sets a review date

essays.stem: A welder suggests skipping slag removal between passes on multi-pass fillet welds, 'because the next pass burns it out'. Explain how you would judge this idea, what you would decide, and how you would respond so that he keeps offering ideas.
essays.modelAnswer: I would judge any idea against safety, quality, the WPS and the client's standard first, then cost and time. Slag left between passes is not reliably burned out; it can be trapped as slag inclusions and cause lack of fusion, which weaken the weld and can fail inspection or fail in service. The WPS and good practice require each pass to be cleaned before the next. So the idea would cost more in repairs and risk than it saves in time, and I would not accept it. I would thank the welder for thinking about saving time, explain the reasons clearly, and, if useful, show him a cut and etched test piece with trapped slag. Then I would ask him to help find another way to save time, such as a better chipping tool, a needle scaler, or a better weld sequence. This way he learns why, and still feels his ideas are welcome.
markingPoints: Judges ideas on safety, quality, WPS and standards before cost and time
Explains why the idea is unsound (slag inclusions, lack of fusion)
Decides not to adopt it
Thanks him and explains clearly, perhaps with evidence
Invites him to find a safe way to save time

essays.stem: Explain how a fabrication shop can use client complaints, inspection reports and near-miss reports as sources of improvement, giving an example for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Each of these records shows where the shop's process is letting it down. Client complaints show problems the shop may not see itself. For example, if several clients say gates arrive with chipped paint at the hinges, the shop can look at how gates are packed and loaded, and add padding and better strapping. Inspection reports, from the shop's own inspector or the client's, show weld and dimension faults. If they show porosity again and again, the shop can tally the defects, use a Pareto chart and fishbone to find the cause, such as damp electrodes, and fix it with an oven and a new store rule. Near-miss reports show accidents that nearly happened. If a plate slips from a lifting clamp, the shop can check the clamps, the training and the lifting method before someone is hurt. In each case the shop should record the problem, find the root cause, make and trial a change, check the result, and share the lesson with the team.
markingPoints: Explains why these records are valuable sources
Complaint example with a sensible improvement
Inspection report example with a sensible improvement
Near-miss example with a sensible improvement
Process: record, root cause, trial, check and share

practical1.title: Measure, analyse and improve a repeat fabrication task with a simple jig (PDCA)
practical1.brief: Your group will improve a repeat job: tacking up small rectangular frames (for example 300 × 200 mm from 25 × 25 mm angle or flat bar) to the drawing the assessor gives. Plan: two members make two frames the usual way (marking and squaring by hand) while another times each step and a fourth measures the finished sizes and diagonals; together, record the baseline and draw a simple process map of the steps, marking any waste. Do: as a group, design and make a simple fit-up jig from scrap (stops and clamps on a plate or table) and agree the new method. Every member helps make the jig. Check: the members who did not tack the first frames now make two frames with the jig, while the others time and measure them. Act: compare before and after on a simple chart, decide whether to keep the jig, write a one-page standard method for using it, and present the results to the assessor as the shop manager. Each member signs the part they recorded. Photograph each stage.
materials: Angle or flat bar cut to length for at least four frames, and a drawing (from the assessor)
Scrap plate, bar and clamps for the jig
MMAW or MIG set for tacking, in a screened booth, with full PPE for every member
Steel rule, tape, engineer's square and stopwatch or phone timer
Record sheets, chart paper and a standard method template
photos: The baseline: a frame being marked and squared by hand, with the timer running
The process map with waste marked
The jig being made, with each member taking part
A frame being tacked in the jig
The frames measured, with the diagonals checked
The before-and-after chart and the written standard method
checklist: Recorded times and measurements accurately for the baseline
Helped draw the process map and identify waste
Took part in designing and making a jig that holds the parts accurately
Tacked frames safely, in full PPE, to the drawing
Measured and compared before and after results correctly
Helped write a clear standard method and draw the chart
Presented results and the decision with reasons
safety: Weld and tack only in screened booths, with full PPE
Treat tacked frames and the jig as hot; use tongs and gloves
Use grinders with guards fitted and the right discs
Keep the area clear of anything that can burn; an extinguisher at hand

practical2.title: Inspect defective weld samples, analyse the defects and present an improvement plan (role play)
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a set of 20 to 30 welded samples from 'last month's production' (coupons or short welds with a mix of faults such as porosity, undercut, slag, lack of fusion and wrong size), and an inspection record sheet. Part 1: each member inspects a share of the samples by eye and with a fillet gauge, marks each fault with chalk and tallies it on the group's check sheet. Part 2: together, draw a Pareto chart of the faults and work out the share of the top two. Part 3: two members draw a fishbone diagram for the top fault, and two members do a '5 whys' for the second fault; all members suggest causes. Part 4: write a PDCA improvement plan for the top fault: the target, the change to trial, who does what by when, how results will be measured and the cost of any equipment (prices from the assessor). Part 5: present the plan to the assessor as the shop manager, who will challenge it. Every member presents one part and signs the part they wrote.
materials: 20 to 30 welded samples with planted faults (from the assessor)
Fillet weld gauges, magnifying glass, chalk or paint markers
Check sheet, Pareto chart paper, fishbone and 5 whys templates
PDCA improvement plan template and a price list (from the assessor, made-up figures)
Gloves and safety glasses for handling the samples
photos: The samples laid out, with faults marked in chalk
Members inspecting samples with the gauge
The Pareto chart with the top-two share worked out
The fishbone diagram and the 5 whys
checklist: Inspected their samples carefully and named each fault correctly
Recorded faults accurately on the check sheet
Drew the Pareto chart correctly and worked out the top-two share
Suggested sensible causes on the fishbone or in the 5 whys
Helped write a plan with a target, a trial, owners, dates and a measure
Did not suggest any change that weakens safety, the WPS or quality
Presented their part clearly and answered the manager's questions
safety: Wear gloves and safety glasses when handling samples; edges may be sharp
Do not grind or cut samples unless the assessor allows it, with guards and full PPE
Keep the room tidy and walkways clear
Speak respectfully when challenged in the presentation
